blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array `nums`, rotate it to the **right** by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative. One step moves the last element to the front. Do it **in place** with O(1) extra space.

blocks.alt: Rotating [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] right by k = 3 gives [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]: the last three elements move to the front.

blocks.text: Example
Understanding the problem
Rotating right by `k` means the **last `k` elements** move to the front, in the same order, and everything else shifts right by `k`.

Rotating by the array's length `n` puts every element back where it started. So rotating by `k` is the same as rotating by `k % n` — with `n = 7` and `k = 10`, only 3 steps actually matter. Always reduce `k` first.
Brute force
The literal approach moves one element at a time: take the last element, shift everything else right by one, put it at the front — and repeat that `k` times.
Each step costs O(n), so the total is **O(n · k)** — too slow when both are large. Copying into a second array, `result[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]`, is O(n) but needs **O(n) extra space**.
The key insight: three reversals
Reversing an array in place is cheap and easy (two pointers swapping inward). And a rotation can be built from three reversals:

blocks.alt: Three reversals on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] with k = 3. Reverse all: [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Reverse the first 3: [5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Reverse the rest: [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4].
blocks.caption: Reversing everything moves the last k elements to the front — they just come out backwards, which the next two reversals fix.

elements.text: blue block is now at the front,
elements.originalText: blue block is now at the front,

blocks.text: Why does it work? Reversing the whole array swaps the two blocks' **positions** — the last `k` elements land at the front — but it also flips each block **internally**. The next two reversals flip each block back, leaving the blocks swapped and correctly ordered.
Dry run it yourself
Each phase highlights the segment being reversed. Try a `k` bigger than the array length and watch it shrink to `k % n` first.
Code
C++'s `std::reverse` does exactly what our helper does, so the C++ version uses it directly.
Complexity

blocks.alt: One step at a time: O(n·k) time and O(1) space. Three reversals: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: Every element is swapped at most twice across the three reversals: **O(n) time, O(1) space**.
Edge cases to test

items: **k = 0** or **k = n** — the array doesn't change.
**k larger than n** — `k = 10` on 7 elements behaves like `k = 3`.
**k = 1** — only the last element moves to the front.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

Rotating **left** by `k` uses the same three reversals in a different order (reverse the first k, reverse the rest, then reverse everything). The "reverse, then reverse the parts" trick also reverses the **words** of a sentence in place, which you'll meet in the two pointers chapter.
